title: JESUS SAW WHAT EVERYONE ELSE APPLAUDED—AND CALLED IT HYPOCRISY
paragraphs: JESUS SAW WHAT EVERYONE ELSE APPLAUDED—AND CALLED IT HYPOCRISY
The Terrifying Warning of Matthew 6:1: When Your Good Deeds Impress Everyone but the God Who Knows Your Heart
What if the very thing people admire about your Christianity is the thing Jesus is asking you to repent of?
Read that again.

What if the prayers people praise you for, the generosity everyone celebrates, the sacrifices everyone notices, and the spiritual image you have spent years protecting are hiding something you have never had the courage to confront?
What if you have become so good at looking faithful that you have forgotten what it means to be faithful when nobody is watching?
There is a warning Jesus gave that should make every Christian examine their heart.
Not just pastors.
Not just worship leaders.
Not just people with thousands of followers posting Bible verses and inspirational messages.
You.
Me.
Anyone who has ever done something good and secretly hoped somebody would notice.
And the frightening part?
You can be doing something genuinely good while nurturing a motive that is spiritually destructive.
You can give money to the poor and still be feeding your pride.
You can pray beautiful prayers and still be performing for an audience.
You can serve in church and quietly become resentful because nobody thanked you.
You can speak about humility while desperately wanting people to recognize how humble you are.
And the people watching may never know the difference.
But Jesus does.
Listen carefully to His words:
“Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven.” — Matthew 6:1, KJV
That sounds severe.
Because it is.
But before you assume Jesus was condemning every public act of righteousness, we need to understand what He actually said.
Because misunderstanding this passage can lead Christians into two opposite mistakes.
Some turn their faith into a performance.
Others become afraid to express their faith publicly at all.
Jesus was warning against neither visibility itself nor genuine public obedience.
He was exposing something much deeper.
The desire to use righteousness as a stage on which the self becomes the star.
And to understand how devastating that warning really is, we need to look at the original language.
In the Greek text of Matthew 6:1, Jesus begins:
Προσέχετε δὲ τὴν δικαιοσύνην ὑμῶν μὴ ποιεῖν ἔμπροσθεν τῶν ἀνθρώπων πρὸς τὸ θεαθῆναι αὐτοῖς.
Prosechete de tēn dikaiosynēn hymōn mē poiein emprosthen tōn anthrōpōn pros to theathēnai autois.
A close translation is:
“Be careful not to practice your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them.”
Notice those words.
“In order to be seen.”
That is where the warning strikes.
The Greek verb θεαθῆναι (theathēnai) comes from theaomai, meaning to look at, behold, or observe. In this sentence, it refers to being seen by others.
The issue is not merely that someone witnesses your obedience.
The issue is that their attention has become your objective.
Jesus is confronting the purpose behind the performance.
And suddenly this ancient warning becomes painfully modern.
Because we live in a world where almost everything can become a performance.
Even faith.
A Bible beside a cup of coffee can become content.
A prayer can become a caption.
A donation can become an announcement.
A moment of worship can become a video.
None of those things is automatically sinful.
A testimony shared publicly can glorify God. A Christian message online can encourage someone who is losing hope. A visible act of generosity can inspire others to help.
But there is a question we cannot afford to avoid.
Would you still do it if nobody liked it, shared it, commented on it, or knew your name?
Would you still pray if there were no one to hear your words?
Would you still give if your contribution remained anonymous?
Would you still serve if somebody else received the credit?
Would you still follow Jesus if obedience cost you the admiration you have grown accustomed to receiving?
That is where the sermon stops being about somebody else.
And starts reaching into our own hearts.
Because some of us do not struggle with whether we believe in God.
We struggle with whether we can obey God without being admired for it.
There is a particular kind of exhaustion that comes from maintaining a spiritual reputation.
You always have to appear strong.
Always have to sound wise.
Always have to seem patient.
Always have to know the right Bible verse.
People come to you because they think you have everything together.
They see your ministry.
They see your service.
They see your encouraging posts.
They see your smile on Sunday.
But they do not see what happens when you close the door.
They do not see how empty you sometimes feel.
They do not hear the prayers you struggle to finish.
They do not know how deeply you crave reassurance that your life matters.
And perhaps, without realizing it, you have begun using the approval of people to quiet an insecurity that only the grace of God can truly address.
That is a painful place to live.
Because applause can become addictive.
And applause is a terrible substitute for communion with God.
Jesus continued:

“Therefore when thou doest thine alms, do not sound a trumpet before thee, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, that they may have glory of men. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.” — Matthew 6:2, KJV
Imagine that.
A person gives something valuable to someone in need.
The hungry are fed.
The poor receive help.
The act itself may genuinely benefit another human being.
Yet Jesus warns that the giver may have already received the reward they were seeking.
Why?
Because the giver wanted human glory.
The Greek expression translated “they have their reward” is:
ἀπέχουσιν τὸν μισθὸν αὐτῶν
Apechousin ton misthon autōn.
The verb apechō can convey receiving something in full. In this context, Jesus is declaring that those who perform righteousness for human praise have received the reward they sought.
The applause was their payment.
The admiration was their prize.
The recognition was what they wanted.
And they got it.
But what a devastating exchange.
To gain the approval of people while forfeiting the reward Jesus promised from the Father for sincere devotion.

It is important to understand that Jesus is not teaching that God's acceptance can be purchased through good deeds. Salvation is by grace through faith, not a reward earned through religious performance (Ephesians 2:8–9).
He is teaching that our motives matter before God.
And that is what makes His warning so searching.
Because the person who wants to be admired for being righteous may receive exactly what they want.
And discover that it was never enough.
There is another Greek word in this passage that deserves our attention.
ὑποκριταί (hypokritai).
Hypocrites.
The word was used for people playing roles, including actors in theatrical settings. In Matthew 6, Jesus uses it to condemn religious pretense.
Someone presenting an outward appearance of devotion that does not correspond to the true purpose of their heart.
Think about that image.
An actor can cry without experiencing the character's sorrow.
An actor can speak words of love without loving the person addressed.
An actor can portray courage without facing the danger.
And a religious hypocrite can display the outward signs of devotion while seeking something other than God's glory.
That is the tragedy Jesus is exposing.
Not every public prayer is hypocrisy.
Not every public donation is vanity.
Not every Christian content creator is performing.
But whenever the desire to be admired becomes the controlling motive of our obedience, something has gone terribly wrong.
And Jesus loves us too much to leave that deception unchallenged.
Perhaps you remember a time when your faith was simpler.
You opened your Bible because you were hungry for God's Word.
You prayed because you needed Him.
You helped people because you remembered how merciful He had been to you.
You worshiped because Jesus was worthy.
Then, somewhere along the way, people started noticing.
They complimented your faith.
They admired your wisdom.
They praised your generosity.
And slowly, almost invisibly, something changed.
You began thinking about how your obedience looked.
You became conscious of who was watching.
You started measuring spiritual fruit through public response.
And when nobody noticed your sacrifices, disappointment began creeping in.
Maybe even bitterness.
You found yourself thinking:
“After everything I have done, nobody even appreciates me.”
That sentence can reveal something important.
Not necessarily that your service was false from the beginning.
Not necessarily that your exhaustion is sinful.
Sometimes people really are neglected, mistreated, or taken for granted, and it is right to seek help and healthy boundaries.
But sometimes our disappointment reveals that human recognition has quietly become part of what we believe we are owed.
Jesus invites us to examine that possibility.
Not to crush us.
But to free us.
Because you were never created to live chained to the opinions of people.
You were created to know and glorify God.
Now here is something that makes Matthew 6 even more powerful.
Just one chapter earlier, Jesus said:
“Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.” — Matthew 5:16, KJV
Wait.
In Matthew 5, Jesus tells us to let people see our good works.
In Matthew 6, He warns us not to practice righteousness to be seen by people.
Is that a contradiction?
Not at all.
It is one of the most beautiful distinctions in the Sermon on the Mount.
In Matthew 5, people see the good works and glorify the Father.
In Matthew 6, the person performs the good works to receive glory from people.
The same outward act can be connected to radically different intentions.
One says, “Look at what God has done.”
The other secretly hopes, “Look at how spiritual I am.”
One points beyond the servant to the Savior.
The other uses service to build a reputation.
And this distinction matters enormously for anyone sharing the Gospel publicly.
Public ministry is not the enemy.
Self-glorification is.
The question is whether Christ remains central, whether the message is truthful, whether financial appeals are honest, and whether people are being served rather than exploited.
John the Baptist captured the heart of genuine ministry when he said:
“He must increase, but I must decrease.” — John 3:30, KJV
That is the posture we must continually return to.
Not “How can I become more impressive?”
But “How can Jesus become more visible through my life?”
Not “How many people admire my faith?”
But “Are people being drawn toward the truth of Christ?”
Not “Will people remember my name?”
But “Will they remember His mercy?”
And this is where the teaching becomes deeply personal.
Because Jesus does not merely tell us what to avoid.
He shows us another way to live.

“But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.” — Matthew 6:3–4, KJV

The familiar wording “reward thee openly” appears in the KJV, but the earliest Greek textual witnesses support the shorter wording that the Father who sees in secret will reward you, without specifying “openly.”
That distinction matters.
Jesus is not promising that every secret sacrifice will eventually become publicly celebrated.
He is promising something better.
Your Father sees.
The One who knows what nobody else knows.
The One who sees beyond the performance.
The One who understands the hidden cost of obedience.
He sees.
The Greek expression ὁ βλέπων ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ (ho blepōn en tō kryptō) speaks of the One who sees in secret.
And perhaps those words are exactly what someone reading this needs tonight.
Because not everyone struggling with this passage is hungry for applause.
Some people are simply tired of being invisible.
You have cared for someone who cannot repay you.
You have given quietly when you barely had enough yourself.
You have prayed for a family member who keeps breaking your heart.
You have forgiven someone who never apologized.
You have served faithfully without recognition.
And somewhere inside, you have wondered whether any of it matters.
Listen to the words of Jesus.
Your Father sees.
He sees the obedience that never became a testimony video.
He sees the tears that never became a social media post.
He sees the kindness nobody photographed.
He sees the repentance nobody applauded.
He sees the lonely battle against temptation.
He sees the quiet choice to tell the truth when lying would have been easier.
And He sees the moment you whisper, “Lord, I am trying to follow You, but I am tired.”
You do not need to manufacture an audience to make your obedience meaningful.
God is not absent simply because people are unaware.
But there is something even more important than knowing that God sees our good deeds.
He also sees our sin.
Our mixed motives.
Our hidden pride.
Our selfish ambition.
Our need for recognition.
And if Matthew 6 ended there, we might walk away terrified that our hearts are too divided to ever please Him.
Because who among us can claim perfectly pure motives?
Who has never wanted recognition?
Who has never enjoyed being praised?
Who has never struggled with pride, even while doing something good?
That is why this teaching must lead us to the Gospel.
Not merely to self-improvement.
Not merely to trying harder to look humble.
Not to the exhausting project of becoming a more convincing religious person.
But to Jesus Christ Himself.
The only perfectly righteous Savior.
The One who never needed to manipulate a crowd to prove His worth.
The One who refused to turn obedience into a spectacle for selfish glory.
The One who lived in complete submission to His Father.
Philippians 2:5–8 tells us that Christ humbled Himself, taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross.
Consider the contrast.
We sometimes want to be elevated for our sacrifices.
Jesus willingly humbled Himself for our salvation.
We sometimes want people to admire our goodness.
Jesus bore the shame of the cross to redeem sinners.
We sometimes use religious activity to protect our reputation.
Jesus endured public humiliation while accomplishing the Father's saving purpose.
And when He died, He did not die merely to provide an inspiring example of humility.
He died for our sins.
He bore the judgment sinners deserve.
He rose again.
And through repentance and faith in Him, guilty people can receive forgiveness and new life.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not that we finally become impressive enough for God to accept us.
But that Christ saves sinners who could never earn their own righteousness before Him.
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21, KJV
Do you see how extraordinary this is?
Jesus exposes our religious hypocrisy, but He does not leave repentant sinners without hope.
He calls us away from performance and into genuine fellowship with the Father.
He does not merely say, “Stop pretending.”
He offers grace that makes honesty possible.
You can confess the pride.
You can admit the envy.
You can acknowledge that sometimes you wanted the attention more than you wanted to honor God.
You can repent of using ministry, generosity, prayer, or spiritual knowledge to elevate yourself.
And you can come to Christ without pretending you are better than you are.
Because the Gospel does not require you to maintain a flawless public image.
It calls you to trust a flawless Savior.
That is what makes grace so beautiful.
It does not excuse hypocrisy.
It gives hypocrites a reason to stop hiding.
It does not celebrate pride.
It offers forgiveness and transformation to those willing to turn from it.
It does not teach us to despise good works.
It restores good works to their proper purpose.
Ephesians 2:10 reminds us that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
We are not saved by our good works.
We are saved for a life in which good works flow from God's grace.
And when that truth settles into your heart, something begins to change.
You can serve without demanding applause.
You can give without needing to announce the amount.
You can pray without trying to impress people with your vocabulary.
You can share Scripture without turning every interaction into a competition for attention.
You can celebrate someone else's ministry without feeling threatened.
You can accept correction without believing your entire identity has collapsed.
You can be unknown to the world and still be deeply known by God.
That is freedom.
Not the freedom of never being tempted by pride again.
But the freedom to recognize it, confess it, and return to Christ.
And perhaps this is where the most uncomfortable question must be asked.
If Jesus removed every visible reward from your Christian life, would you still want Him?
If following Him brought no popularity, no impressive title, no public recognition, no admiration, and no earthly advantage, would He still be enough?
Do not rush to answer.
Because sometimes the most spiritual-sounding answer is the one we have rehearsed rather than the one our hearts are actually living.
Sit with the question.
Let it search you.
Then remember Peter.
Peter was a disciple who genuinely loved Jesus, yet he also failed Him terribly.
He spoke confidently of his loyalty.
Then, under pressure, he denied knowing his Lord.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine the memory of his own promises.
Imagine the terrible distance between the man he thought he was and the man his fear revealed.
But Peter's failure was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him and called him again to care for His sheep (John 21:15–19).
The risen Christ did not build Peter's restoration on the illusion that Peter had never failed.
He confronted him with love and recommissioned him for service.
That is a picture of grace worth holding close.
Because perhaps your own heart has been exposed while reading this.
Maybe you realized that you have been seeking attention through your faith.
Maybe you have been measuring your worth by how many people recognize your sacrifices.
Maybe you have been more concerned about maintaining your reputation than cultivating your relationship with Christ.
Maybe you have used spiritual language to conceal a desperate hunger for validation.
Or perhaps you have been wounded by religious people who seemed more interested in being admired than in loving others.
Whatever brought you here, do not miss the invitation of Jesus.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Stop defending what God is calling you to surrender.
And receive the mercy that is found in Christ.
You do not have to turn your repentance into another performance.
You do not need to post an emotional confession to prove that you are sincere.
You do not need to tell the whole world every private struggle.
Godly repentance can begin in the quiet place where nobody is watching.
And when repentance calls for making something right with another person, have the courage to do that too.
Because genuine righteousness is not simply private.
It is sincere.
Sometimes it is visible.
Sometimes it is hidden.
But it seeks the glory of God rather than the glory of self.
And that brings us to something important about Gospel Warrior and why this ministry exists.
We share Scripture, biblical teaching, encouragement, conviction, and discipleship resources publicly because the truth of Jesus Christ is worth proclaiming.
Not because a public platform makes anyone more righteous.
Not because engagement numbers measure someone's spiritual value.
But because God's Word can be shared with people who desperately need to hear it.
Somewhere, there is a father who has quietly stopped praying.
A mother who feels spiritually exhausted.
A young believer struggling with temptation.
A person who has been hurt by religious hypocrisy.
Someone who has confused church attendance with knowing Christ.
Someone who thinks their past is too shameful for forgiveness.
And someone who is one honest encounter with the Gospel away from realizing that the door of mercy has not been closed to them.
We cannot change their hearts.
Only God can do that.
But we can faithfully proclaim His Word.
We can place biblical truth before them.
We can point them to the Savior who forgives sinners and transforms lives.
And if this article has helped you see the words of Jesus more clearly, consider what it could mean for someone else who is struggling with the same hidden battle.
Not to prove that you are spiritual.
Not to collect praise for sharing Christian content.
But because someone among your family, friends, or followers may need this reminder.
And if this message has exposed something in your own heart, I would love for you to respond with honesty.
You do not need to disclose private sins or painful details publicly.
A simple, sincere response can become an opportunity for prayer, encouragement, and fellowship.
And if you have experienced God's grace in this area, your testimony may strengthen someone who feels trapped by shame.
Return to it when pride begins whispering that your obedience only matters if someone notices.
Return to it when comparison steals your joy.
Return to it when you feel invisible.
Return to it when you are tempted to measure your relationship with God through the reactions of other people.
Not everyone who encounters a Christian message will immediately embrace the Gospel.
But everyone deserves to hear the truth of Christ presented faithfully and lovingly.
There is also a deeper way to help sustain this work.
It is a practical way to participate in the ministry's mission.
But I want to make something unmistakably clear, especially in light of Matthew 6.
Your salvation cannot be purchased.
God's love is not for sale.
And the amount of money someone gives is not a reliable measure of their spiritual maturity.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, thoughtful, and free from compulsion.
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
Your responsibilities to your family, your local church, and those in genuine need matter.
Give with wisdom.
Give with joy.
Give because you believe the work is worth supporting.
And if you cannot give financially, please know that your prayers, thoughtful encouragement, and willingness to share faithful biblical teaching are deeply meaningful.
It is about helping people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
These items can serve as reminders of biblical truth, gifts of encouragement, and practical resources for discipleship.
But they are not the reason to follow Christ.
Jesus Himself is the treasure.
These resources are intended to help believers deepen their understanding of Scripture, grow in prayer, strengthen their faith, and pursue a more Christ-centered life.
And because the library includes free resources, financial support should never be confused with purchasing access to God's grace or earning a place in His family.
If you pray for this ministry, thank you.
And if all you can do today is open your Bible and return to Jesus with a sincere heart, that matters more than any engagement statistic ever could.
Because this entire message would lose its meaning if we used Jesus' warning against religious performance to pressure people into another kind of religious performance.
That is not the Gospel.
The Gospel is the good news of what God has done through His Son.
And the purpose of every faithful Christian ministry must be to direct people back to Him.
Before you leave, I want you to imagine something.
The day comes when the applause of this world is silent.
Your followers cannot speak for you.
Your reputation cannot defend you.
Your achievements cannot purchase your salvation.
Your public image cannot conceal your heart.
And you stand before the God who knows you completely.
What will matter then?
Not how convincingly you played the part of a righteous person.
Not how many people thought you were holy.
Not how carefully you protected your spiritual image.
What matters is whether you belong to Jesus Christ.
Whether your hope rests in His finished work rather than your own performance.
Whether the faith you profess is genuine.
And whether the grace you received has begun transforming the way you live.
The Christian's ultimate confidence is not in having performed enough righteous deeds to impress God.
It is in the Savior who died and rose again.
And because He is our Savior, we can pursue obedience without turning it into a desperate attempt to earn acceptance.
We can love without keeping score.
We can give without demanding recognition.
We can serve without making ourselves the center.
We can confess our failures without despairing.
And when pride returns, we can return to the cross.
Maybe tonight your prayer needs to be simpler than it has been in a long time.
“Father, forgive me for the times I wanted people to notice me more than I wanted them to see You.
Forgive me for the times I made obedience about my reputation.
Forgive me for the times I resented being unseen.
Forgive me for the times I looked righteous on the outside while hiding selfish motives within.
Thank You that Jesus Christ died for sinners like me.
Thank You that His resurrection gives me hope.
Teach me to love what You love.
Teach me to serve with sincerity.
Teach me to give without pride.
Teach me to pray without performing.
And when nobody sees what I do, remind me that You are enough.
Let my life point to Jesus.
Not to my goodness.
Not to my reputation.
But to His mercy.
In Jesus' name, amen.”
And now, perhaps for the first time in a long time, you can stop trying to prove that you are somebody.
You can simply belong to Christ.
You can do the next faithful thing.
Even if nobody notices.
Even if nobody thanks you.
Even if nobody applauds.
Because the deepest joy of following Jesus is not that the world finally recognizes how good you are.
It is that, despite knowing how sinful you are, the Savior offers forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and a transformed life through His grace.
And that is why the story does not have to end in the scandal of our hypocrisy.
It can lead to the grace of our Redeemer.
The world may never applaud the moment your heart finally surrenders—but the Savior who died for you sees what no audience ever could.
